# Research notes on 1 Corinthians 11, verse by verse

**Gaps:** My searches turned up nothing from these sources: Wesleyan sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Pentecostal and charismatic sites other than Enduring Word, Orthodox sources (oca.org), bibleodyssey.org, NET Bible notes, or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. So those views are left out. Verses 8–9, 11–13 and 33–34 have only thin coverage. Some Bible Hub and StudyLight comments don't say which old commentator wrote them, so I describe those as unattributed notes.

---

**v. 1:** Paul could tell the Corinthians to copy him because he knew he was following Jesus. In practice it means "follow me as far as you see me following Jesus." Guzik thinks the verse most likely belongs with chapter 10, though Paul was a good example either way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/

**v. 2:** Guzik reads Paul's praise as sarcastic: the Corinthians didn't really remember him in everything or keep the traditions. The "traditions" are the apostles' teaching received from Jesus, not ceremonies or rituals. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/
- Dan Wallace argues that verse 2 shows the practice Paul defends was more than a local habit. When someone looks just at 1 Cor 11:16, a good case could be made that the practice … may well have been no more than a community-wide habit. Once, however, v 2 is examined, it is evident that v 16 is saying much more. https://bible.org/article/what-head-covering-1-cor-112-16-and-does-it-apply-us-today

**v. 3:** Guzik grants that "head" can mean "source." But he argues it carries the full sense of headship and authority, and that being under authority does not make someone inferior. Christ is fully under the Father yet fully God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/
- GotQuestions calls verse 3 the key to the passage. The order is: God the Father, God the Son, the man or husband, and the woman or wife. The veil or covering on the head of a believing Corinthian wife showed that she was under the authority of her husband. It also says the passage does not teach that women are inferior. https://www.gotquestions.org/head-coverings.html
- Thomas Schreiner answers those who read "head" as "honor" or "source": All the lexical evidence suggests that the word head means authority. https://bible.org/seriespage/head-coverings-prophecies-and-trinity-1-corinthians-112-16

**vv. 4–6:** Guzik says the head covering was a public sign of being under someone else's authority and protection. A man praying covered would be saying "I am under others' authority," which dishonors Christ. A woman praying uncovered would be saying "I am not under authority." He quotes Adam Clarke's claim that only prostitutes went unveiled. He also quotes Gordon Fee warning against picturing a full Muslim-style veil, which is unknown in ancient evidence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/
- **Shaving (v. 6):** Guzik says a shaved head marked adultery in Jewish law and could mark a prostitute in the Greek world. In effect Paul says, "If you throw off the covering, go all the way." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/ GotQuestions adds that a shaved head was a disgrace and, in Jewish thinking, a sign of mourning. https://www.gotquestions.org/head-coverings.html
- Ligonier notes the view that Paul may have wanted to protect Christian women from charges of immorality, since prostitutes in Corinth advertised their "trade" with uncovered heads. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/principle-or-custom
- Benjamin Merkle (The Gospel Coalition) sees the issue as blurring the difference between men and women. He compares a woman going uncovered to a woman adopting a man's hairstyle. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/should-women-wear-head-coverings/
- Thomas Constable (bible.org) concludes that the Corinthian women seem to have rejected the concept of subordination within the church, along with its cultural symbol. https://bible.org/question/what-does-head-covering-1-cor-11-refer
- Bob Deffinbaugh points out that "praying or prophesying" is said of men and women alike. If both are doing the same thing, the head covering is what distinguishes them. https://bible.org/book/export/html/802

**v. 7:** Guzik gathers older comments on "woman is the glory of man." Trapp says either the man may glory in a good wife or she gives him honor. Poole links it to Adam's words, "bone of my bone." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/
- Merkle says the creation argument in verses 7–9 mainly explains how man is God's image and glory and woman is man's glory. It does not directly require head coverings. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/should-women-wear-head-coverings/

**vv. 8–9:** Guzik says the order of creation came before the Fall, so the difference in roles in church and home is not removed by new life in Christ. He applies "woman for man" to Genesis 2:18, where Eve is made as Adam's helper. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/

**v. 10:** Interpreters admit this is very hard.
- **"Sign of authority":** Luther (quoted in the Bible Hub notes) says *exousia* means "the veil or covering, by which one may see that she is under her husband's authority." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/11-10.htm Constable takes the opposite line: *exousia* is a liberating word, the sign of the woman's own authority to take part. https://bible.org/question/what-does-head-covering-1-cor-11-refer Gill notes the reading that the word means her power to put the covering on or off as circumstances require. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/11-10.htm
- **"Because of the angels":** Guzik (and Poole, whom he quotes) says angels are present when Christians worship and notice any departure from reverent order. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/ Calvin, Barnes and Constable note the range of views: good angels, evil angels, or human "messengers." Constable rejects the idea that evil angels lusted after women, asking why women wouldn't then need veils everywhere. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-corinthians/11-10.html
- Some honestly admit they don't know. Barnes calls it one of the very few pass ages in the Bible whose meaning as yet is wholly inexplicable. The Geneva Study Bible says, "What this means, I do not yet understand." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/11-10.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary mentions the Jewish tradition, followed by Tertullian, that angels fell through lust for women (Genesis 6). It still prefers the reading of reverence for the holy angels present in worship. https://biblehub.com/1_corinthians/11-10.htm
- **Catholic (Cornelius à Lapide):** Lapide rejects the idea of Justin, Clement and Tertullian that angels could be stirred to lust. He says angels are witnesses of women's modesty and obedience. https://studylight.org/commentaries/clc/1-corinthians-11.html
- Guzik argues that none of the three reasons (headship, creation, angels) depends on culture, though how they are applied may vary. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/

**vv. 11–12:** Schreiner says verses 3–10 defend male headship while giving women full participation in worship. Verses 11–12 then qualify the argument: Woman and man stand in interdependence in the Lord. https://bible.org/seriespage/head-coverings-prophecies-and-trinity-1-corinthians-112-16

**vv. 13–15:** Guzik reads verses 13–16 as an appeal to experience, nature, common sense and apostolic authority. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/
- Ligonier (following Sproul) says Paul is not setting a fixed hair length. He is noting that, by nature, women generally have longer hair, which shows a covering is fitting. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/long-hair-for-a-covering
- Constable explains that long hair was a woman's "glory" because it showed the difference between the sexes. Her natural covering supports wearing a physical one. He also describes the alternative view that hair *replaces* a separate covering. https://bible.org/question/what-does-head-covering-1-cor-11-refer
- Merkle says the argument from nature shows that male–female differences are part of creation's design. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/should-women-wear-head-coverings/

**v. 16, and whether coverings apply today (the main debate on vv. 2–16):**
- **Required today:** Ligonier (Sproul) says that because Paul grounds the practice in creation, the practice should be followed in every generation. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/long-hair-for-a-covering Deffinbaugh (bible.org) says head covering is a command, a tradition which was to be followed by every woman in every church. https://bible.org/book/export/html/802
- **Principle stays, symbol changes:** Wallace sets out three views (doesn't apply; the covering is hair; a real covering still required). He argues that in the West today a covering would humiliate women, so some suitable substitute symbol needs to be found. https://bible.org/article/what-head-covering-1-cor-112-16-and-does-it-apply-us-today Schreiner and Merkle (TGC) both hold that the covering's meaning was cultural and is not required now, while male headship remains. https://bible.org/seriespage/head-coverings-prophecies-and-trinity-1-corinthians-112-16 · https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/should-women-wear-head-coverings/
- **Optional:** GotQuestions says a woman may choose to wear one as a sign of submission. https://www.gotquestions.org/head-coverings.html
- These lines don't follow denominations neatly: Reformed writers (Ligonier and TGC) disagree with each other here.

**vv. 17–22:** Steven Cole explains the setting. Churches met in wealthier members' homes for a shared meal (the Agape, or "love feast") before the Supper. The rich arrived first and ate, the poor and slaves found nothing left, and some got drunk. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34
- GotQuestions: The Corinthians' communion services had become corrupted with selfishness, drunkenness, and discrimination against the poor. https://www.gotquestions.org/take-communion-unworthily.html
- **v. 19:** Cole says most commentators read this as God bringing good out of bad, letting factions reveal who is truly mature. Against the majority, he (with the NLT and J.B. Phillips) reads it as sarcasm. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34
- **v. 20:** For Cole, their selfishness cancelled the meaning of the meal. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34 The Catholic Haydock commentary (quoting Challoner) says "the Lord's supper" here means the charity feasts, which were held together with the Eucharist. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-corinthians-11.html

**v. 23:** Cole notes this is the earliest written account of the Last Supper. Scholars differ over whether Paul received it by direct revelation or through the apostles; Cole thinks direct revelation. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34

**vv. 24–25, "This is My body" (where traditions really differ):**
- **Symbolic or memorial (evangelical/Baptist-style):** Cole understands Jesus was speaking symbolically: the elements picture Jesus' body and blood. Christ is spiritually present, but no more than in preaching. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34 A TGC sermon stresses that the disciples looked back to the cross, not to the bread. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/discussion-on-communion/
- **Reformed:** Ligonier says the passage points toward affirming that Jesus is really and spiritually present (the snippet I saw was cut off at that point). https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lords-supper-and-examination
- **Lutheran:** The LCMS teaches that "the very body and blood of Christ… is actually present in the Sacrament," quoting the Small Catechism: "It is the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ under the bread and wine." https://reporter.lcms.org/2024/close-closed-closed-communion-three-words-one-meaning/
- **Catholic:** A Catholic Answers article argues that "remembrance" (*anamnesis*) means more than a mental act. It says the bread is called Christ's body because it contains that body. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/does-paul-teach-the-real-presence-of-christ Guzik summarizes transubstantiation as the bread and wine actually becoming Christ's body and blood. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/
- **New covenant (v. 25):** Cole links it to Jeremiah 31:34, God promising to remember sins no more. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34

**v. 26:** Cole notes the word for "proclaim" is the same one used for preaching the gospel. He says the Supper implies the resurrection, since Jesus can't return unless he was raised. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34 The LCMS says remembrance isn't just calling Jesus to mind but a participation in His body and blood. https://resources.lcms.org/reading-study/preparation-for-the-sacrament-christian-questions-with-their-answers/

**v. 27, "unworthy manner":**
- Guzik says the KJV word "unworthily" has misled people into thinking they must make themselves worthy. In fact the repentant sinner is the one who most needs the Supper. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/
- GotQuestions thinks Paul most likely meant failing to show love and unity, the problem he had just described. https://www.gotquestions.org/take-communion-unworthily.html
- Ligonier: unworthily partaking of the bread and wine makes us liable for Christ's death. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/examining-ourselves
- Gill (on StudyLight): such a person dishonors an ordinance that symbolizes Christ's body and blood. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/glt/1-corinthians/11-27.html
- **Catholic:** The Catholic Encyclopedia argues there could be no grievous offense against Christ himself unless his true body and blood are really present. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/05573a.htm Catholic Answers argues similarly from Paul's "homicide" language. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-most-straight-forward-verse-about-the-eucharist-in-the-bible

**v. 28:**
- **Lutheran:** The LCMS ties self-examination to "close communion" (sharing the Supper only with those of the same confession). People who come should know what they are receiving, so it is for their forgiveness and not their harm. https://reporter.lcms.org/2024/close-closed-closed-communion-three-words-one-meaning/ Another LCMS article says that examining yourself will always show your need for forgiveness. https://witness.lcms.org/2020/the-closed-communion-conversation/
- Cole calls it a private inventory of your relationship with Christ. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34 GotQuestions calls it a "heart check." https://www.gotquestions.org/examine-yourself.html

**v. 29, "recognizing the body":**
- **Body = the church:** Ligonier says that, in context, it must refer in some way to harmony in Christ's body. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/lords-supper-and-examination An unattributed note on Bible Hub links it to the church as Christ's body (1 Cor 12:27). It says the Lord's body is discerned by the soul in faithful receiving, *not present in the elements themselves*. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/11-29.htm
- **Not telling the Supper apart from an ordinary meal:** This is Gill's reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/11-29.htm An unattributed StudyLight note says it means failing to distinguish this meal from common meals, not some spiritual perception of the body in the elements. https://www.studylight.org/bible/ger/lut/1-corinthians/11-29.html
- **The Lord's body and blood:** Cole holds this view. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34
- **Catholic:** Guzik reports that Catholics use this phrase to support transubstantiation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-corinthians-11/
- **Text and wording:** An unattributed Bible Hub note says "the Lord's" is missing from the best manuscripts, and that "judgment" (KJV "damnation") does not mean final condemnation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_corinthians/11-29.htm

**vv. 30–32:** Cole says the sickness and death were the Lord's discipline, not eternal condemnation, because of their unloving and irreverent conduct. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34 GotQuestions says the purpose of self-examination is to avoid that discipline. https://www.gotquestions.org/take-communion-unworthily.html

**vv. 33–34:** Cole places these verses with verses 17–22 as part of coming to the Supper with love for others. He urges people to put right broken relationships before taking part. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-11-how-come-lord-s-supper-1-corinthians-1117-34
